title: AegisBid Omega
subtitle: Bacula backup, verified disaster recovery and durable auction engineering

blocks.text: Primary contribution: Bacula-backed, independently checked recovery. The implementation combines durable auction decisions, audit evidence, consistent database exports and isolated restoration. Selected successful workload experiments are reported on page 6.

blocks.text: Durability and trust contract

QUEUED means committed SQL intake, not final acceptance. Each UUID binds one immutable bidder/auction/amount tuple. Accepted bids are evaluated in order; winners are allocated only after eligible pending work drains. Backup correctness is established by restoring and verifying data, rather than by a successful job status alone.

Verification includes 39 backend tests, Go race/concurrency checks, selected full-request workload replays and controlled recovery drills. The comparison helper is an in-memory race demonstration; a real legacy-system benchmark remains outside the measured scope.

Blue arrows trace bidding and decision authority. Gold/green paths protect and restore committed data. Bacula operates on prepared consistent artifacts; it is separate from the live bidding path. Recovery is verified in isolation before any promotion decision.

blocks.text: 2. Consistency before media backup

Issue: a dump and independently collected counts could represent different database states. Solution: the exporter holds a read-only REPEATABLE READ transaction, obtains pg_export_snapshot(), and passes that snapshot to pg_dump -Fc. Counts and auction sequence positions share the checkpoint. A manifest records the dump SHA-256, schema version and checkpoint time.

SQL snapshot -> custom-format dump + manifest -> /staging
Director -> File Daemon -> Storage Daemon -> media + Catalog
3. Scheduling, retention and secret handling

AegisSchedule defines a Sunday 02:00 Full job and Monday-Saturday 02:00 Incremental jobs. AegisPool uses 30-day volume retention, at most 30 volumes and 2 GB per volume; Catalog file/job retention is 30/90 days. These file jobs protect prepared exports; exporter freshness and continuous WAL protection are separate concerns.

Runtime credentials replace template placeholders. The local profile exposes no host ports and keeps media, Catalog and daemon state on persistent volumes. An export is recorded as EXPORTED; it is marked Bacula-completed only after an actual successful Catalog job is imported.
Configuration: infra/bacula/bacula-dir.conf, bacula-fd.conf, bacula-sd.conf; infra/compose.bacula.yaml; scripts/backup_export.py and record_bacula.py.

Recorded outcome: backup and restore completed normally. Job 1 (AegisBidBackup) and Job 2 (AegisBidRestore) both recorded JobStatus T, four Catalog entries and 39,802 bytes. The restored database then passed checksum and independent ledger/winner checks.

blocks.text: 3. Restore certificate and measured scope

The JSON/HTML certificate records the backup ID, protected checkpoint, counts, checksum result, verification outcome and duration. This drill proves the recovered 20-request dataset. The 1.25218 s timer excludes operator response, Bacula media retrieval and site rebuilding. RPO is unmeasured without an actual failure timestamp; this drill did not check an external signed anchor.

Production recovery must also protect the Catalog, daemon configuration, media index and encryption/signing keys on an independent recovery domain. The local single-host Bacula rehearsal validates backup/restore mechanics; independent-site survival requires a separately operated deployment.
1. Price races, retries and allocation

Issue: concurrent offers and retries can create contradictory decisions. Safeguard: PostgreSQL serializes each auction decision prefix; globally unique UUIDs bind immutable payloads and changed reuse returns 409. BIGINT cents avoid floating-point amounts. Required price is max(reserve, high + increment); final allocation ranks distinct offers by amount descending, then decision sequence.
2. Worker failure and admission ordering

Sorted UUID locks and sequence reservation permit parallel admission. An exclusive worker intake barrier waits for earlier admissions before capturing the next prefix; it is released before evaluation. A new boot has a new holder, a five-second lease and increasing epoch. Decisions, offers, request states, hash events and a batch-version outbox notification commit together.
3. Late requests and publication gaps

New requests after cutoff receive terminal CLOSED receipts outside the sealed ledger; prior UUID retries retain their original result. Legacy stranded rows are repaired. SQL command_queue separates broker publication metadata from queued business rows, while reconciliation recovers commands not delivered through JetStream. Tests check terminal history and unchanged winners/anchor.
4. Identity, evidence and live delivery

Salted scrypt protects passwords; four-hour HS256 sessions require subject, issuer and expiry. Cookies, origin checks and role/owner checks protect access. The private admission endpoint requires an independent key and verifies every session. Go groups up to 512 bids per RPC and shares bounded live snapshots. SHA-256 chains and optional Ed25519 manifests support independent rule/winner replay; unsigned exports are INCOMPLETE.
5. Operational controls

Prometheus/Grafana expose queue, decision, lease and gateway signals. Test-only chaos uses fixed actions without an API Docker socket. Per-process quotas bound overload; predictive pre-warming and fleet-wide controls remain production work. The corrected failure harness restarts only the worker container, preventing an unintended migration restart during the fault experiment.

Both selected historical HTTP-only experiments passed their complete run gates. For these recorded runs, request coverage was 100%: 50,000 distinct users, 50,000 original requests and 50,000 final audited outcomes. This percentage describes these experiments, not every release or deployment.

Test setup and measured scope

Five generators pre-issued real sessions and offered one bid per user over nine seconds. HTTP pooled at most 5,120 connections on one 12-CPU / 7.46-GiB host. These runs measure admission during the final window; queued decisions drain afterward. SQL row timestamps are not exact commit-visibility instants.

The normal run and worker-kill run are identified by prefixes 6a341563 and 93aedc3e; both used source commit f607529. Full run IDs, image hashes and replay commands remain in the repository bidding-proof records.

blocks.text: How the recovery layers complement Bacula

Replication handles a short primary failure; Bacula preserves prepared recovery artifacts; WAL enables recovery beyond a logical snapshot; remote encrypted copies address local storage loss. Backup credentials stay outside application services. A valid restore requires data and key recovery plus ledger/allocation verification, not simply a successful download or daemon restart.
Deployment and capacity limits

The 50k results on page 6 are selected historical passes for their recorded configuration. Later-layout repeatability and combined live-feed/bidding capacity remain unresolved; the current branch is not certified for reliable 50k operation. Physical three-zone EKS was configured/validated but not launched. The real S3 vault uses the configured account. Independent-account backup and continuous production offsite PITR/RPO remain unproven.
Bacula-centered three-minute demonstration

Show the system flow, place a small live bid, then display Bacula jobs 1/2 with T status and the restored database certificate. Highlight checksums, 20 decisions, 21 events and 3 winners. Present the two labelled historical 50k successes and run offline signed replay. Finish with terminal late-request behavior and the deployment scope. Use recorded recovery evidence rather than restoring over the live app.
